newsitem.title: INDIA: Indians cast peaceful vote for change in Punjab.
newsitem.headline: Indians cast peaceful vote for change in Punjab.

text.p: Voters in India's northern state of Punjab voted on Friday in elections that were widely expected to eject the Congress party from power.
The state's chief electoral officer Brajendra Singh said except for a minor skirmish between supporters of Congress and its arch-rival Akali Dal party, polling had been peaceful.

Officials said the elections to the 117-seat Punjab state legislature were the first in two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatist violence. They said voter turnout was likely to be a high 60 percent in comparison with past elections.
"We expect the voting to be around 60 percent," said Tilak Raj Sarangal, district chief of Ludhiana, Punjab's business hub.
India poured in 100,000 paramilitary soldiers to oversee elections. Police tightened security and sealed the borders of Punjab state with Pakistan.
Punjab police chief Sube Singh said all vehicles entering the rich farming region were searched for weapons.
Most opinion polls have predicted a victory for former chief minister Prakash Singh Badal's pro-Sikh Akali Dal party.
Even the ruling Congress party admitted it would lose its majority. The party won 87 seats in February 1992, mainly because of an Akali Dal boycott.
But Congress politicians were sanguine. "No party is expected to get a majority," said Malkiat Singh Dakha, a minister in the outgoing government and Congress candidate from a Ludhiana constituency.
"The Congress will get 50 seats," Dakha said. His aides said privately the figure could be exaggerated.
Most of the voters at polling stations in Ludhiana said they were unhappy with the rise in food prices during five years of Congress rule.
"For me that is the main issue," said Kusum Devi, a young housewife at the polling station in the Habbowal area.
Others hailed the return of peace to Punjab.
"This is the first time I have dared to vote in an election," said Shailendra Kumar, a 30-year-old car mechanic, as he waited for his turn at a polling booth in Ludhiana.

Kumar, a Hindu, said his family was cautious about expressing political opinions for fear of annoying the state's Sikh separatists whose guerrilla war against Indian rule in Punjab resulted in more than 20,000 deaths in over a decade.
"Everyone knows that the political climate has changed dramatically, so we decided to cast our vote," Kumar said, looking at his family members in the small queue behind him.

"I am suprised at the enthusiasm of the voters as I have received reports of long queues at almost all polling stations before the voting started at 7.30 a.m. (0200 GMT)," election official Brajendra Singh said.
Polling stations closed at 4.30 p.m. (1100 GMT). Around 15.2 million voters were eligible to vote, officials said.
Sikh separatist violence peaked after Indian troops were sent into the Golden Temple in Amritsar in 1984 to flush out militants holed up in the Sikhs' holiest shrine.

The showdown triggered a bloody spate of violence in the state. The then prime minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984, in what is believed to be a revenge killing for the army assault.
State polls in 1992, which revived local democracy after more than a decade of separatist violence, were held in an environment of fear and overbearing security.
The counting of ballots in Punjab is expected to start on Sunday and results are likely to be announced on the same day, officials said.
